newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says N.Korea food stocks will run out June 20.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says N.Korea food stocks will run out June 20.

text.p: With malnutrition rising rapidly in North Korea, U.N. agencies warned on Wednesday that the government will have no food stocks left by June 20.

Catherine Bertini, director of the Rome-based World Food Programme, told a news conference the government's food rationing system had nearly collapsed and people were facing starvation, with isolated cases of deaths due to malnutrition already having been reported.
Introducing a WFP and Food and Agriculture Organisation report, Bertini said international food aid to North Korea has only covered a small part of the need.

WFP far this year has appealed for 200,000 tons of food or about $95 million, about 72 percent of which has been raised. But Bertini said the country required 1.8 million tons to avoid large-scale starvation.
Five government distribution centres had already run out of foodstuffs in May and the remining five would do so by June 20, according to the report.

Wednesday's warning was the most serious in recent weeks on the food shortage that resulted from two years of flooding which ruined farmland. The damage was particularly severe because trees had been cleared for firewood and agriculture.
Bertini said the new harvest could be good because of favourable weather conditions, but that young crops had already been taken from the soil for immediate needs.
Under the most optimistic scenario, the report forecast about 4 million tons, which would be substantially below requirements for the following year.
Bertini said WFP had raised 144,464 tons of food and negotiations for more were currently under way with the European Community, Germany, Canada, France and New Zealand.
Countries and other groups donating aid directly raised another 180,108 tons.

Donors have been slow to contribute large amounts of food because there are not enough international observers to monitor it and because of distaste for the country's authoritarian community government. Diplomats also point out that many nations awaited South Korea's lead in donating aid.

People have survived on bark, dried vegetable leaves, ground corncobs and ground sweet potato stalks. Small irregular farm markets had formerly provided some food, but most have closed as surpluses have dwindled.
